docs.title: BLV 3D Printers
docs.text:
Open-source 3D printers by Ben Levi - an archive of the BLV mgn Cube, BLV Ender 3 Pro and BLV mgn12 projects.

I'm an open-source 3D printer developer. The BLV projects are my way of saying "thank you" to the 3D community I admire. Here you'll find guides, assembly videos, instructions, BOM, sketches, original CAD files and all the information you need to build your own BLV 3D printer. BLV projects are non-profit and free for non-commercial use.

Sincerely yours,Ben Levi

docs.title: About me
docs.text:
Design with your heart, make with your mind, and share with those who taught you...

My story is very simple. Many years ago I gained my 3D knowledge from the old community forums. Every single comment and thread was gold to me and to others, building the basics of what we all have today.

Making each BLV 3D printer project was really hard and took 300+ hours. It wasn't easy, especially with a lovely wife, two wonderful little kids and a day job that has nothing to do with 3D printing. But this "thing" is my therapy... I think. It heals my soul and gave me back the passion I thought was lost.

I really don't mind sharing my work. 11 years ago the FDM 3D printer patent expired, and sharing experience is the base of everything we have now. Imagine if we had none of it, and everyone kept their findings and work to themselves.

I hope this gives you an idea of what I believe in, my friends...

Sincerely yours,Ben Levi

docs.title: BLV Ender 3 Pro
docs.text:
UPGRADE MOD

I'm very excited to introduce my BLV Ender 3 Pro upgrade project, designed for the popular Ender 3 Pro 3D printer. Its goal is to take your beloved Ender 3 Pro to the next level: with all-aluminum parts, MGN12 linear rails, a BMG dual drive extruder and more, you get maximum accuracy, efficiency and print quality.

Download all files Thingiverse Remixes Facebook group

Where to get the BLV Ender 3 kit: Big Tree Tech store · Unique3D · Blurolls - HIWIN rails · FYSETC store · Victory3D · Shenjiang · LYXcnc

BLV Ender 3 ProBLV Ender 3 Pro - print sample

docs.title: Why build it
docs.text: Fast, reliable, accurate Linear bearings and Delrin wheel gantries are common in low and mid range printers because they are cheap, but they cost accuracy and reliability. Linear guided (MGN) rails are much more rigid, extremely precise and smoother - shorter print times without losing quality. That's why high-end printers use them. I found cheap Chinese MGN rails on AliExpress and thought: why not? If you're tired of worn POM wheels and constantly tightening them, you came to the right place. Rigid parts This time I chose a different path. Printed parts are a bit flexible, and I wanted to take that out of the equation. CNC machined parts take the printer to the next level of accuracy. To test it I used a BT dial indicator logging into a database on my PC: after more than 2000 measuring loops of uniformity and deviation, the aluminum parts clearly improved the results compared to printed parts. Accessible CNC machined parts are expensive, right? To make the kit cheaper, I give all my work free for commercial use under one condition - my permission. Part of the cost of such parts is the design time (more than 200 hours here); saving that lets manufacturers sell the kit cheaper. For example, while 4 aluminum parts sell for $30+ on AliExpress, this kit has 16 pieces for $59, including belts, screws and shipping. Other aluminum + rails kits cost $300 and more. Now, I bet you're asking yourself something... Open source Where's the catch - why is this guy giving his work for free? A couple of years ago I got all my 3D knowledge from this awesome community. I really appreciate it and love this hobby, so this is my way of giving back - the same reason I made my earlier projects, the BLV mgn Cube and the BLV Anet mod. It's not easy, with a precious wife, 2 lovely little kids and a day job that has nothing to do with 3D printing. But this "thing" is my therapy (I think ☺️). 10 years ago the FDM patent expired, and sharing experience is what built everything we have now. Imagine if we had none of it and everyone kept their findings to themselves... I hope this gives you an idea of what I believe in, my friends :)

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Read, understand and prepare yourself - read the project description, watch the 3D animation videos and make sure you understand the printer structure.
  2. Get the parts - all the parts in the BOM, spare T-nuts and screws, and the tools you need. Also, mentally prepare yourself :)
  3. Build - now the fun begins. A precise structure is crucial for excellent prints; several YouTube videos show how to align the Ender 3 Pro frame. Use the provided jigs when installing the MGN rails - it makes the assembly much easier. Take your time fixing the rails to the extrusions: this quick video by 3D Distributed shows an easy way to align parallel rails.

  4. Electronics - if you install the SKR Mini E3 V1.2 board, there's an excellent YouTube installation guide. It's the same with the Duet WiFi 1.04 board (if you're crazy enough).

    SKR Mini E3 installation guide

  5. Software, tests and calibrations - the scary part: you must know what you're doing, or follow the thousand YouTube videos on calibrating the Ender 3 Pro. My advice: replace the original firmware with a fresh Marlin, following one of the YouTube masters. Don't skip:

    • Wiring check + endstop check
    • Firmware update (a freshly updated Marlin)
    • Extruder calibration
    • Feed rate calibration
    • Hotend PID
    • Bed PID
    • Probe Z offset / Z offset
  6. Print - enjoy your printer and give it love when needed :) Grease the rails with white lithium grease or light sewing machine oil, keep the rails clean and the belts tight. Clean the PEI build plate with alcohol after every print, and scratch new sheets a bit with brass wool.
  7. Post an "I made one" - show the world your new printer and be proud of your creation :) I'd really appreciate pictures of your build; knowing it helped you makes all the hours worth it.
  8. Remix and share - I'm 100% sure there are many ways to make this printer better, which is why the source file is included. Make it better and share your remixes with this awesome community :)
  9. Want to make it? For commercial use, read the legal license.

docs.title: Hotend
docs.text:
I highly recommend upgrading to a decent hotend. First decide: stay with Bowden, or go direct drive?

BowdenDirect drive
  • The original Creality hotend | cheap hotend clone
  • High quality hotend by Mellow
  • Excellent quality hotend by Trianglelab
  • Dragon V2 hotend - amazing results!

Trianglelab DDE direct drive - 24V full kit - an amazing system!

Its X carriage is very similar to the original Ender carriage. To install the DDE you need to drill two small holes for M3×6 mm screws in the carriage - a 2-minute job (how).

Use the two screws for alignment only, then remove them.

docs.title: Z axis
docs.text:
Choose your Z setup:

  1. Single Z stepper - I used this for a while and was satisfied, but dual Z adds even more rigidity and dramatically improves the Z axis.
  2. Dual Z with one stepper - dual Z kit: one stepper, 2 threaded rods and a belt. Gain back some lost Z height with this BMG bracket. I lost some height (the extruder touches the left top plate), but this became my favorite. Replace the kit's original Phillips screws with hex socket head screws from a local shop.
  3. Dual Z with two steppers - this is the recommended kit for dual Z with an additional Z motor. Align the Z axis to match on both sides.

Note

This method reduces the Z height, since the BMG can touch the top plates.

docs.title: Belts
docs.text: The original Creality belt is too flexible and hurts print quality. The kit comes with a fiberglass-reinforced GT2 6 mm belt, which is much better. The X-axis belt is clamped at a length of 785 mm (the belt between the clamps, not including the brass clamps). If you need to replace a belt, you can lock both ends with a zip tie.

docs.title: Build volume adjustment
docs.text: To keep the original build volume, change Y_MIN_POS in Marlin's Configuration.h. My calculation came to -9.15; adjust it to your needs. The picture shows where to find it.

docs.title: Dual Z - move the PSU
docs.text:
With the dual Z option, the PSU has to move:

  1. Disconnect the PSU from the wall.
  2. Disconnect the PSU from the printer.
  3. Partly remove the plastic cover from the PSU.
  4. Drill M5 holes as shown below.
  5. Insert 3 × M5 8 mm button head screws + T-nuts.
  6. Put the plastic cover back on the frame and tighten the screws.
  7. Put the PSU back and lock it to the cover.

docs.title: Smart filament sensor
docs.text:
What's so special about the SKR smart filament sensor? At first I was confused: why pay $15 when a wire and an endstop switch cost $1.5? After watching this video I understood the potential.

A switch sensor only knows whether filament is there. If the spool jams or the filament gets stuck - nothing happens, and the printer keeps printing air. The smart sensor tracks the filament movement with a rotary encoder: if it suddenly jams, the print pauses. Worth every cent, especially for huge prints (12+ hours). A big like for this smart filament sensor!

docs.title: PEI surface
docs.text: After a long time with the Energetic PEI spring steel sheet, I tested the new Trianglelab double-coated PEI spring steel sheet. It came well packed with alcohol wipes and - yes - a printed manual. The first try was a complete fail: the corners lifted. Then I read the manual, and the last tip did the trick: scratch the PEI really well with brass wool, and prints stick great. And unlike the Energetic PEI, prints release easily once the sheet cools down.

docs.title: LED installation
docs.text:
Use a 5V, 60 LEDs/m, non-waterproof strip that can be cut after every LED - the non-waterproof type slides into the V-slot channel more easily.

  1. Cut a 15-LED strip, solder a long 4-wire cable to it, and slide it into the top V-slot channel.
  2. Cut a 3-LED strip, solder a cable to it, and secure it with 2 zip ties to the back of the transparent BMG extruder.
  3. Connect both strips together and check the connection.
  4. Then either:
    • connect them to an RGB LED controller (simple) and use the IR remote, or
    • connect them to the SKR Mini E3 LED pins and configure it.

docs.title: Rail tips
docs.text:
I used cheap Chinese MGN12H rails from AliExpress at $18 each. After buying from 4 different sellers, I found the best rails at the "CNA Mechanical Parts Store". I didn't even need to clean them - the blocks slide smoothly. Wonderful rails, highly recommended!

Stores to avoid

Don't buy rails from "RDC Official Store" or "linkcnc Store" on AliExpress. linkcnc sold me a used, damaged rail, shorter than ordered - it stayed stuck even after cleaning and lubricating. RDC started shipping MGN blocks in non-standard sizes.

Cleaning and lubricating. New rails won't be as smooth as they should be: they're coated at the factory with a protective oil that must be cleaned off (YouTube has videos on cleaning the carriage with WD-40). Then lubricate the rails and carriages with sewing machine oil or Teflon silicone grease - not thick grease, these are miniature rails. Ignore the "tilt the rail" smoothness test - it's wrong. You want them smooth, but not too smooth.

Cleaning an MGN12H carriage - video - a pretty good one. Use a container so you don't lose the steel balls. After reassembly there will be an empty space of one ball; that's normal.

Fixing the MGN rails can be very frustrating: they must be perfectly aligned and straight, or you'll get headaches. Don't start this project without tons of patience.

docs.title: BLV mgn Cube
docs.text:
OPEN-SOURCE 3D PRINTER

The BLV mgn Cube is an open front CoreXY 3D printer built on MGN linear rails, for maximum accuracy, efficiency and print quality. The goal of the project is simple: to let anyone build a good, reliable 3D printer.

1.78Mdownloads6.3Mviews29/10/22last update

Start building Download the files

BLV mgn Cube 9000 mm/s² acc, 500 mm/s - ultra fast 3D printing

docs.title: Ways to build it
docs.text:
You can source every part yourself, or start from one of the kits below. The BOM page walks you through the choice.

  • Full kits - all the needed parts in one package

    FYSETC full kit (recommended) or the Blurolls kit.

  • Metal Kit - replace your 3D printed parts with aluminum parts

  • Blind Joints frame - new improved frame, 20 minutes assembly

docs.title: Why build it
docs.text: Fast, reliable, accurate Linear bearings and Delrin wheel gantries are common in low and mid range printers because they are cheap, but they cost accuracy and reliability. MGN linear rails are more rigid, more precise and much smoother, which cuts print time without hurting quality. That is why high-end printers use them. When I found cheap Chinese MGN rails on AliExpress, I thought: why not? Rigid open structure The open front is as rigid as a closed cube, but gives easy access to the build plate and prints. A front belt tensioner makes it even more convenient. The design came out of many hours of software simulation and physical stress tests. Accessible All parts are easy to source, print or craft. There are no expensive or hard-to-get CNC parts in the BOM - and where there are, they are surprisingly cheap. You can use your own electronics, as long as you know how to adjust the firmware to the build. Open source The original CAD files (STEP) are included in the project folder - no need to ask. Feel free to modify, remix or improve them. I would appreciate it if you share your changes with the community and mark the parts as "remixed", linked to this project page. Build and print I spent many hours tuning the firmware and the slicing profile (Simplify3D) for this printer. After the build you only need to upload the config files, load the profile and you are good to go. Modular The printed parts and the structure are modular: both the Z height and the build plate can grow. All you need is longer aluminum profiles and MGN rails. The included CAD file helps you calculate the measurements for your custom size. Easy to build? Honestly, installing the rails takes about 70% of the build time. You need to be precise and spend a few hours aligning them - but the joy when it prints is worth every minute. To make it easier, I made 3D animation videos, information PDFs, sketches and measurements. Balanced budget The BOM is balanced for the best value without compromising quality: a top 32-bit board, excellent stepper motors and sensors. You can choose a 5" PanelDue touch screen, or save $80 and use your smartphone or tablet without losing any features.

docs.text:
The original BLV mgn Cube had official Bowden and direct drive options. The Metal Kit has a Bowden option with twin blowers, and direct drive setups for the BIQU H2 and the Trianglelab Matrix.

But that's not all - the amazing community behind the project made a huge variety of hotends for every version, even a tool changer. Check the community remixes and choose the hotend that fits your needs. These drawings of several BLV hotend versions help with the assembly and with the exact auto-leveling coordinates.

  • BLV Cube tool changer

  • EVA 2.3.0 supported

The whole idea of the project is to benefit the 3D community, so it's no surprise that many of the best solutions come from the community itself. I gathered the best upgrades, remixes and new features in one place:

Community remixes

docs.title: Reinforcement for taller Z builds
docs.text: If you build taller than the standard height, add a 496 mm reinforcing extrusion at the top, just below the front tensioners, as in the picture. It keeps the frame stable even on tall builds.

docs.title: Air scrubbers - HEPA + activated carbon
docs.text:
The project has a small and a large air scrubber. Printing releases particles into the air we breathe, so filtering them is a good idea.

Mount the fan so it pushes the dirty air into the filter: the air passes through the activated carbon filter first, then the HEPA filter. Check the filters once a month and replace them when needed.

docs.title: Magnetic heated bed
docs.text:
The most recommended bed is an aluminum MIC6 plate with an AC silicone heater. It has two problems:

  1. High price - both the MIC6 plate and the silicone heater are relatively expensive.
  2. Risk of electric shock if it isn't installed properly.

So the safest option is a 24V bed - slower than AC heating, but safe. The FYSETC kit comes with a magnetic aluminum heated bed with a BuildTak-like glass surface: flat and easy to handle. The original Blurolls kit comes with a PCB bed, which I recommend less because it tends to warp at high temperatures - message the seller and ask to replace it with his upgraded magnetic metal bed.

These pictures are from the FYSETC kit (see my FYSETC kit unboxing). You can also get the bed from the BOM. Install the magnetic surface layers exactly in the order shown.

docs.title: Internal lights - COB LED strip
docs.text:
After a long time with a regular LED strip, I wanted lighting that is nicer, hidden, needs no printed parts, and shines evenly instead of in spots. The answer: a COB LED strip.

A COB strip packs much smaller diodes: about 360 LEDs per meter instead of 60 - six times more - so the light is uniform. The diodes are covered in silicone that acts as a diffuser. The strip is also narrow; I chose 8 mm, which slides right into the extrusion channel. It can be cut every 50 mm, and the brightness can be controlled.

My first two strips from different AliExpress stores were disappointing. Then I found a reliable store with quality COB strips. I chose: 6000K cool white, 24V, 360 LEDs, 2 meters.

  1. Cut the strip at the marks (every 50 mm) with scissors.
  2. Solder two 26AWG wires - or use this fast connector (choose "For 8 mm PCB") if you can't solder.
  3. Slide the strip into the upper extrusion channels.
  4. Connect the wires in one of two ways:
    • Directly to a 24V PSU
    • To a Duet fan output - then you can control the brightness with a slider in the Duet control panel

I use the FYSETC Duet 3 6HC board, so I defined the lights as a fan output with this line in config.g, and connected the strip to the OUT9 port:

M950 F2 C"out9" Q500 M106 P2 S0.2 H-1 C"Lights"

I'm very pleased with the result: efficient, good-looking light whose intensity I control from the panel.

docs.title: Linear rails - assembly tips
docs.text:
At first I used cheap Chinese MGN12H rails from AliExpress at $18 each. After buying from 4 different sellers, I found the best cheap rails at the "CNA Mechanical Parts Store": the block slides smoothly without cleaning. Wonderful rails if you want a cheap solution. For higher quality, the HIWIN linear rails kit from Blurolls is not that expensive and very, very good.

Stores to avoid

Don't buy rails from "RDC Official Store" or "linkcnc Store" on AliExpress. linkcnc sold me a used, damaged rail, shorter than ordered - it stayed stuck even after cleaning and lubricating. RDC started shipping MGN blocks in non-standard sizes.

docs.title: Cleaning and lubricating
docs.text:
New rails won't be as smooth as they should be: at the factory they are coated with a protective oil that must be cleaned off. Some YouTube videos show how to clean the carriage with WD-40. After cleaning, lubricate the rails and carriages with sewing machine oil or Teflon silicone grease. These are miniature rails, so don't use thick grease. You want them smooth, but not too smooth.

The video below is a good one - just work over a container so you don't lose the steel balls. After reassembling, there will be an empty space of one ball; that's normal.

Tuning up cheap Chinese linear bearings

Fixing the MGN rails can be very frustrating: they must be perfectly aligned and straight, or you'll get headaches. Don't start without tons of patience.

The gravity test - no!

Don't test the rails with the well known "gravity test", where you tilt the rail and let the carriage slide down. It doesn't tell you if the rail is good: a rail with excessive free play passes it easily - and then fails every print quality test. The rail's tolerance grade determines how much friction the carriage has.

docs.title: Decision 1: Metal Kit or printed parts?
docs.text:
A large part of the printer is printed. Printing the parts saves money but takes a long time and some skill. After the project came out I released the BLV Metal Kit - an aluminum kit that replaces most of the printed parts and is stronger, more reliable and more accurate. The Metal Kit is the recommended choice.

docs.title: Calibrations
docs.text:
Before calibrating, make sure the right firmware is on the Duet board. When the project was released the Duet ran RepRap 2.x; it later moved to the Duet 3 board with RepRap 3.x. For the Duet 2 WiFi, our dear friend David Husolo did amazing work on his BLV Cube config on GitHub: compatible, well-calibrated config files for both the Duet 2 WiFi and the Duet 3 running RepRap 3.x.

Several steps below point to the excellent Duet guides. With them you can calibrate your board and get to high-quality prints. (My fine-tuned config files were planned to be shared with the new FYSETC kit guide.)

docs.title: 1. Update the Duet firmware
docs.text:
Duet boards are the best documented boards, with step-by-step guides for almost anything. Update to the latest RepRap firmware 3.x before any calibration. The Duet 2 WiFi and the Duet 3 share the same update guide.

Download the firmware Update guide

docs.title: 2. Copy the config files
docs.text:
Copy the BLV config files to the SD card. If the card is new or empty, follow this guide first to rebuild the Duet SD card.

Your setup Config files RepRap 3.x (recommended) David Husolo's GitHub, in the "firmware" folder - thank you David for the amazing work! FYSETC kit FYSETC firmware for the BLV mgn Cube Old RepRap 2.x The SD card ZIP in the project files (one ZIP is a basic Duet 3 config, the other is for RepRap 2.x only)

docs.title: 3. Connect to the web interface
docs.text:
The Duet has a built-in web interface that gives you complete control of the printer. This guide helps you set up the network and access the board:

Network setup guide

Do's and don'ts - avoid damaging your hardware

  • Never disconnect cables from the Duet while it is powered, except the USB cable.
  • Check all wires and avoid shorts - especially fan, motor and heater wires.
  • Don't feed the board more than 24 volts.
  • Ground the extrusion frame and the bed carriage - and the motors too if you can.
  • Don't scratch, short or damage the electronics while installing them.
  • Don't remove the memory card while the printer is running.
  • Take your time crimping connectors and check the wires with a multimeter.
  • Triple check that "+" and "-" wires are plugged in properly and in the right place.
  • With the steppers connected, don't move an axis by hand fast enough to spin the motors quickly.

docs.title: 4. Configure your printer
docs.text:
The provided config files cover almost everything, but you may want final changes: centering the bed, motor directions, macro buttons, temperature presets per filament and so on. The Duet guides cover all of this and more:

  • Full Duet 2 WiFi guide
  • Full Duet 3 guide
  • RepRap 3 overview - must read

Do these before the next step:

  • Center your bed
  • Test your endstop switches
  • Set up a different Z sensor - only if you use another auto-leveling sensor
  • Set up a PT100 sensor - only if you use a PT100 temperature sensor

docs.title: Stepper motors
docs.text:
With the FYSETC kit you can skip this: its plug-and-play cables are labeled, with the wires in the right order for the FYSETC config. If you bought the steppers from the BOM or have the Blurolls kit, the motors probably won't turn the right way (unless you're really lucky). Set them up like this:

  1. Identify the coil (phase) wires. A stepper has 4 wires, 2 per coil, and you need to find the pairs - see this quick guide or this video.
  2. Connect the steppers using the original Duet stepper wiring, shown in the bottom right corner of wiring diagram v3.2 ("Duet original steppers wiring").
  3. Test and configure them according to the Duet documentation. The video shows the expected movement for each command in the Duet guide.
Easily identify the leads of a 4-wire stepper motor with a multimeterBLV mgn Cube 3D printer - steppers test

When the steppers are set up, check the motor directions: in this video I press the jog buttons by hand, and your printer should move the same way.

BLV mgn Cube 3D printer - axis movement

  • Tuning stepper motor drivers - fully tune the Duet's TMC2660 drivers
  • Mesh bed compensation - to change the mesh settings

docs.title: 5. Calibrate
docs.text: These calibrations can't be skipped. Do them exactly as shown in the pictures, with maximum accuracy - they have a huge impact on the results.

docs.title: Hotend PID
docs.text:
The picture shows the classic way to PID-tune the hotend. Newer RepRap 3.x releases add an algorithm that detects fan PWM changes and adjusts the heater in advance. To use it:

  • Run the latest 3.x release.
  • Define all your tools (T0) correctly.
  • Define your fans according to the RRF instructions.
  • Turn off the layer fan, then run M303 T0 S200 - replace 200 with your normal printing temperature. The algorithm turns the fan on by itself while tuning.

In short: replace M303 H1 S190 with M303 T0 S190.

docs.title: 3D printing the parts
docs.text:
How you print the parts has a huge impact on how they work, so follow the instructions closely: orientation, number of walls, printing angle, filament type and even print speed all matter. Most parts are designed to print without supports.

Can I buy a kit of printed parts?

Not everyone has a printer available or the time to print all the parts. Print services are usually expensive because they charge by print time. A cheaper option: an AliExpress store sells BLV mgn Cube printed parts in green PETG with 80% infill - a good solution if you have neither the time nor a printer.

docs.title: The build, step by step
docs.text:
1. Read, understand and prepare yourself Read the project description and the "more info" links, watch the 3D animations and explore the printer in the 3D viewer. Make sure you understand the printer structure before you start.

  2. Get the parts The waiting is the most frustrating part. Make sure you have all the parts in the BOM, plus spare T-nuts, screws and so on. If you use your own electronics, make sure you know how to configure the firmware for your board.

  3. Build This is not as easy as a pre-made kit. Prepare all the tools you need and use a good corner alignment tool - a precise structure is crucial for excellent prints. The provided jigs make the assembly much easier. Tap the holes in the extrusion ends and check whether they take M5 or M6 screws (it depends on the extrusion maker). Take your time fixing the rails to the extrusions: this quick video by 3D Distributed shows an easy way to align parallel rails. And reward yourself after the rails are in - you deserve it :)

  4. Electronics installation Install the electronics carefully. Check every connection against the wiring diagram, don't take shortcuts, and use the right tools and parts. The power cable is the last thing to connect.

  5. Software, tests and calibrations Update the Duet WiFi board to the latest firmware, copy the provided config to the micro SD card, insert it and power up. The Mini IR sensor should blink 4 times right after power-up. Don't move the axes before you check the endstops. Home the printer: it should move to the left and then to the rear - if not, check the motor wiring and config. Calibrate the Z height and check the temperature readings. Run a PID calibration for both the bed and the hotend - this is very important, otherwise your prints will fail. If everything looks good, load filament and print a calibration cube. Details are on the Calibrations page.

  6. Print Enjoy your printer and give it some love when needed :) Grease the rails with synthetic grease with PTFE or sewing machine oil. Keep the rails clean and the belts tight. Clean the PEI build plate with alcohol after every print. If you use the air scrubber, replace the HEPA filter when needed.

  7. Post an "I made one" Show the world your new 3D printer and be proud of your creation :) I would really appreciate it if you upload pictures of your build. Knowing that the project helped you build your own printer makes all the hard work and the many hours worth it.

  8. Remix and share I am 100% sure there are many ways to make this printer even better - that is why the source files are included. Make it better and share your remixes with this awesome community :)

Wiring is a critical step - double check every wire you install. It takes about 3 hours, sometimes more. docs.title: BLV mgn12 mod
docs.text:
FOR ANET A8 / PRUSA I3

The goal of this project: turn your Anet A8 into an incredible 3D printer, with MGN12 rails fixed on an aluminum extrusion frame. The upgrade is compatible with Pheneeny's AM8 mod with small changes. It completely changes your printer - much more reliable, accurate and fast.

Download all files Thingiverse Remixes Facebook group

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Linear bearings and Delrin wheel gantries are common in low and mid range printers as a cheap replacement for MGN rails - but at the expense of accuracy and reliability. Linear guided (MGN) rails are much more rigid, extremely precise and smooth. They let you print faster without losing quality, and because the rails are fixed to the frame, they prevent unwanted motion from bent threaded rods or the other axes. That's why high-end printers use them. So when I found cheap Chinese MGN rails on AliExpress, I thought: why not?

docs.title: Important
docs.text:
Patience required

Fixing the MGN rails can be very frustrating: they must be perfectly aligned and straight, or you'll get headaches. Don't start this project without tons of patience.

  • Design flexibility and source file - I'm sharing the source file so the design can be improved; the STEP file is in the project ZIP. Please follow the license (Creative Commons - Attribution - Non-Commercial - Share-Alike).
  • If you use the STEP file, don't forget to mark your work as a remix :)
  • I also made a build plate for Simplify3D for this project.

Note

You may need to re-center the bed coordinates in the Marlin configuration, or move the Z extrusion to center the hotbed.

Seeing so many great community members upload photos and remixes is worth all the long hours I put into this project :) I'd really appreciate an "I made one" photo :)

docs.title: Mod variations - choose your style
docs.text:
1. Anet A8 converted to AM8 (original height 440 mm) + BLV mgn12 mod - if you already own an AM8 and don't want to change its height, get 350 mm rails instead of 400 mm.

  2. Anet A8 converted to AM8 + taller Z axis (500 mm) + BLV mgn12 mod - build the AM8 with small changes:

    • instead of 2 × 440 mm 2040 extrusions → 2 × 500 mm (or longer) 2040 extrusions
    • instead of 2 × 340 mm 2040 extrusions → 4 × 364 mm 2040 extrusions
    • longer 400 mm threaded rods

    You don't need to print all the AM8 parts - see what to print. 3. Anet AM8 + freestyle + BLV mgn12 mod - the design is flexible, with separate parts you can fit as you wish. For a custom size with a bigger bed or a taller Z axis, choose your extrusion sizes and attach the modular parts to them.

docs.title: Rail tips
docs.text:
I used cheap Chinese MGN12H rails from AliExpress at $18 each. After buying from 4 different sellers, I found the best rails at the "CNA Mechanical Parts Store". I didn't even need to clean them - the blocks slide smoothly. Wonderful rails, highly recommended!

Stores to avoid

Don't buy rails from "RDC Official Store" or "linkcnc Store" on AliExpress. linkcnc sold me a used, damaged rail, shorter than ordered - it stayed stuck even after cleaning and lubricating. RDC started shipping MGN blocks in non-standard sizes.

Cleaning and lubricating. New rails won't be as smooth as they should be: they're coated at the factory with a protective oil that must be cleaned off (YouTube has videos on cleaning the carriage with WD-40). Then lubricate the rails and carriages with sewing machine oil or Teflon silicone grease - not thick grease, these are miniature rails. Ignore the "tilt the rail" smoothness test - it's wrong. You want them smooth, but not too smooth.

Cleaning an MGN12H carriage - video - a pretty good one. Use a container so you don't lose the steel balls. After reassembly there will be an empty space of one ball; that's normal.

Fixing the MGN rails can be very frustrating: they must be perfectly aligned and straight, or you'll get headaches. Don't start this project without tons of patience.
